overview: I3103 is the radar-approach event: precision PAR, nonprecision radar approaches, recommended-altitude control, and emergency decision making while under vectors. The standard is to follow controller instructions promptly without surrendering aircraft control, orientation, minimums discipline, or the propeller-malfunction branch logic.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: PAR is a precision radar approach in which the final controller gives azimuth and glideslope corrections to guide the aircraft to DA/DH.

children.text: Expect surveillance radar vectors toward final, normally with standard-rate turns not exceeding 30 degrees AOB and prompt compliance with assigned headings and altitudes.
Complete landing checks, review minimums, lost-communication instructions, missed-approach or climbout instructions, and keep position orientation with available NAVAIDs.
PAR equipment provides precise runway centerline guidance, elevation guidance, and range; typical training limits are about 10 NM range, 20 degrees azimuth, and 7 degrees elevation.
When transferred to final controller, include gear status if required and be in before-approach configuration before glideslope intercept.
Begin descent only when told "on glideslope," not when told "approaching glidepath."
At glideslope intercept, use about 24 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and roughly 600 FPM. Pitch controls airspeed and power controls glideslope, with small prompt corrections.
At DA/DH, continue only if the runway environment is in sight and the landing is safe; do not level at DA/DH.

If communication is lost for more than 1 minute on vectors to final, more than 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, or more than 5 seconds on PAR final with glideslope, attempt secondary or tower frequency.
Proceed VFR if able, or execute the approved non-radar approach or published radar lost-communication procedure.
Miss immediately if directed by controller, tower, RDO, or wheels watch; if unsafe; or at DA/DH without required visual references.

items.text: PAR W/O GS is a nonprecision radar approach: the final controller gives precise azimuth and range, but no glideslope.

children.text: The approach may start with surveillance radar vectors and then transfer to PAR final for azimuth-only final guidance.
Because no glideslope is provided, the controller states the MAP location and mile markers and may direct descent to MDA or step-down fixes.
The more precise PAR azimuth and range may support a lower MDA than an ASR approach, but it remains a nonprecision approach.
Use about 200 KIAS on downwind and 150 KIAS on base; if extended on final or dogleg, maintain 200 KIAS until within about 15 NM.
Transition to before-approach configuration and complete landing checks on final or dogleg no later than 15 NM.
With recommended altitudes, use about 24 percent torque and 120 KIAS, adjusting descent to meet the altitude gates.
Without recommended altitudes, use about 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM to MDA.
Lead the level-off about 100 feet before MDA, maintain MDA and assigned heading to the MAP, then land only if visual and safe.

items.text: ASR is a nonprecision radar approach using airport surveillance radar for course guidance throughout the approach.

children.text: Expect heading corrections, range calls, the MAP location, and descent instructions to MDA or step-down fixes.
Because the controller is not providing glideslope, you are responsible for a stable descent profile, MDA level-off, and timing the decision at the MAP.
If circling is planned, provide the aircraft approach category when needed so the correct circling MDA is used.
Acknowledge controller instructions unless told not to acknowledge; slow or missed readbacks are a major radar-approach error.
Do not descend to MDA early just to get level. Heavy precipitation and low altitude can increase ground clutter and degrade radar contact.
If radar contact is lost and the runway environment is not in sight, execute the missed approach or assigned climbout.
At the MAP, guidance terminates; if the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe, go missed.

items.text: Recommended altitudes are pilot-requested altitude gates on final that help stabilize a nonprecision radar approach to MDA.

children.text: They are based on the procedure descent gradient and are normally issued at each mile on final down to the last mile at or above MDA.
Use them as a rate-control aid, not permission to descend below published step-down restrictions or below MDA.
With recommended altitudes, adjust descent rate to meet each gate while keeping 120 KIAS and a stable configuration.
Without recommended altitudes, manage your own descent rate, level 100 feet prior to MDA, and maintain MDA until the MAP.

items.text: IMC emergency discussion starts with aircraft control, terrain clearance, ATC coordination, and crew coordination before checklist detail.

children.text: NATOPS procedures are the best available procedures, but they do not replace judgment when weather, terrain, multiple emergencies, or aircraft state change the problem.
Use the basic order: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.
Inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or IMC abort requires a stable instrument scan before troubleshooting expands.

Maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit; squawk as required and tell ATC your intentions.
On an IFR clearance, coordinate deviations with ATC unless the emergency requires immediate action.
A declared emergency and radar vectors to a suitable recovery field may be the safest option; brief what you need from ATC before task saturation takes over.
The pilot at the controls executes critical action memory items and PIC-directed actions while preserving the scan.

items.text: Propeller malfunctions include uncommanded power change, failure to produce expected power, and uncommanded propeller feathering; the branch point is whether enough usable power remains for a PEL.

children.text: Engine rollback may show decreasing power or thrust, decreasing fuel flow and N1 with PMU on, or a step change in power with PMU off.
Uncommanded propeller feathering may show rapid NP decrease, torque increase, increased propeller noise, thrust loss, vibration, and degraded glide performance.
Prop-sleeve touchdown may cause NP fluctuations, torque increase, thrust decrease, vibration, and possible CHIP indication.
Set PCL to mid range, physically halfway between IDLE and MAX, then set the PMU switch OFF.
If NP is stable below 40 percent, pull the PROP SYS circuit breaker. Stable means below 40 percent with no upward change for 3 seconds at constant airspeed and torque.
Expect the propeller to unfeather in roughly 15 to 20 seconds if the procedure is effective.
Use PCL as required after the initial actions, monitoring torque, ITT, NP, and rate of descent.
If sufficient power is available, execute a PEL.

If power is insufficient, consider leaving the engine operating at mid-range PCL only when uncommanded feather is suspected and engine limits remain acceptable; otherwise transition toward engine shutdown, forced landing, or ejection as directed by the checklist and aircraft state.

With the PROP SYS circuit breaker pulled and PMU OFF, the feather dump solenoid is unpowered; the propeller feathers more slowly as oil pressure decreases, and glide performance may be considerably reduced.

If VSI remains greater than 1500 FPM at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and only 4 to 6 percent torque, increase torque as needed up to limits. If unable to reduce descent rate, set PCL OFF.

studyNotes.summary: Fly radar approaches through controller instructions without losing minimums discipline, IMC emergency priorities, or the propeller-malfunction decision tree.

summary: PAR, PAR without glideslope, ASR, recommended altitudes, IMC emergencies, and propeller-malfunction branch logic.
